findings.issue_text: [ADVISORY] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a DB read plus a write (record.save) inside model validation, so every save of any User whose email changed — including failed or repeated submissions — issues an UPDATE to blocked_emails and increments match_count. Operators' match_count/last_match_at statistics are inflated by retries and by attempts that fail other validations, and every user validation that touches an email now carries a synchronous UPDATE on the request path; a stats-driven auto-block heuristic built on these columns later gets garbage data.

[ADVISORY] The guard `record.errors[attribute].blank?` only checks errors added by this validator's whitelist/blacklist branch, so should_block? runs even when the presence/uniqueness validators have already added errors to :email, and the blocked error is appended on top. A user submitting an email that is both already taken and blocked sees two stacked email errors in full_messages ('has already been taken' plus 'is not allowed.'), and the blocked_emails row is still mutated even though the whitelist failure already explained the rejection.

[ADVISORY] should_block? increments match_count via read-modify-write (record.match_count += 1; record.save) with no locking or atomic UPDATE, and ignores the save's return value. Concurrent signups for the same blocked email (e.g. a spam bot firing parallel requests) lose increments, and a validation failure in BlockedEmail's own before_validation/uniqueness check silently drops the stats write with no log — the caller never learns the counter update failed.

[ADVISORY] The client rejects any email in rejectedEmails with the generic 'user.email.invalid' reason, but rejectedEmails is never cleared when the modal is closed or on a new session, and it also catches emails rejected for reasons like 'already taken' (any server email error pushes into the list). A user whose email failed for a transient or fixable reason (e.g. duplicate account, later whitelisted by staff) is told their email is invalid for the lifetime of the Ember app — closing and reopening the signup modal does not clear it — and sees the wrong reason string since the server's distinct 'blocked' message is discarded.

[ADVISORY] The push into rejectedEmails fires for any server error on :email, not only 'blocked' errors, because the check is only `result.errors.email` with no error-type discrimination, while the server deliberately distinguishes not_allowed vs blocked messages. Emails refused due to whitelist/blacklist domain rules or duplicates are permanently cached as locally 'rejected', so the client-side message shown on retry ('user.email.invalid') disagrees with what the server would actually report, and support staff debugging sees inconsistent UX.

[ADVISORY] email_in_restriction_setting? builds an unescaped alternation regexp from raw site-setting text via Regexp.new, so entries containing regex metacharacters (a domain typo like 'foo|bar' or '(' in the admin-entered list) raise RegexpError at validation time. A site admin entering a malformed domain list turns every account creation and every email update into a 500 for all users until the setting is reverted; this flaw was merely moved verbatim from the deleted User#email_validator rather than fixed during extraction.

[ADVISORY] BlockedEmail has no writer anywhere in this diff — no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, seed, or data-entry path creates blocked_emails records — so the feature ships inert. Operators cannot actually block an email without hand-written SQL; the entire BlockedEmail table, validator branch, and client-side rejectedEmails mechanism are dead weight until someone adds an entry path, and no acceptance criterion in the diff verifies the end-to-end block of a real email.

[ADVISORY] The client adds the submitted email to rejectedEmails for any server-side email error, not only a 'blocked' error, so an email rejected for 'has already been taken' is permanently shown as 'user.email.invalid'. A user whose email collides with an existing account retries that same address later (e.g., after the original account is deleted) and the client still refuses it with the generic invalid-email message, plus no client-side test in the diff covers the pushObject branch at all.

[ADVISORY] The new EmailValidator's whitelist and blacklist branches (lib/validators/email_validator.rb lines 6-11) have zero spec coverage — every test in the new spec stubs should_block? and runs with SiteSettings unset, so `email_in_restriction_setting?` and the regexp gsub/escape logic copied from user.rb are never executed. A regression in the migrated domain-restriction logic (e.g., the dot-escaping or case-insensitive regexp construction) would pass the entire suite while breaking whitelist/blacklist signup for every site using those settings.

[ADVISORY] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a write (`record.save`) inside a User validation read-path, so two concurrent signups with the same blocked email race on match_count (lost update) and the save failure is silently ignored because the return value is never checked. Operators inspecting match_count/last_match_at to judge whether a blocked email is being abused get undercounted statistics, and any save failure (uniqueness race, validation drift) silently drops the stats update while the block decision still proceeds.

[ADVISORY] The new errors/values payload is emitted only on the validation-failure branch and has no spec anywhere in the diff (no UsersController create spec, no client test asserting the rejectedEmails push), so the server contract the JS at create_account_controller.js:274-276 depends on is completely unverified. The exact shape `result.errors.email && result.values.email` is untested in both directions — a serialization change (e.g., symbol keys, attribute renaming) would silently disable the client-side rejected-email UX with no failing test.

[ADVISORY] The BlockedEmail check inherits the `if: :email_changed?` gate, so updating any other attribute on a persisted user whose email already lives in blocked_emails passes validation — but the diff also drops the old email_validator's unconditional coverage question without any spec confirming email_changed? is true on User.create. If email_changed? is false on any creation path (e.g., an assignment path that bypasses change tracking in this Rails version), a blocked email sails through signup with no test in the diff to catch it, since the validator spec builds a bare record and calls validate_each directly rather than through User.create.

[BUG] Blocked-email enforcement runs only `if: :email_changed?`, but the whole point of the feature is to stop blocked users, and BlockedEmail.should_block? matches the stored email with an exact case-sensitive string comparison, so the check is bypassable. A user whose email was added to blocked_emails re-registers with mixed-case or trailing-variant of the same address (BlockedEmail.where(email: email) in blocked_email.rb finds no row because the lookup is not downcased/normalized), defeats the block, and the invariant the PR claims to enforce — blocked users cannot create accounts — silently fails.

[ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table and BlockedEmail model ship with no writer anywhere in the diff — no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, seed, or staff controller ever creates a BlockedEmail row. Site operators who deploy this PR have no way to actually block an email address; the feature is inert until a follow-up admin interface lands, and the reviewer cannot trace the end-to-end requirement to any usable path.

[ADVISORY] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a read-modify-write (record.match_count += 1; record.save) inside an ActiveModel validation, so merely validating a user mutates blocked_emails rows. Every validation pass — including retries, failed saves for unrelated reasons, and `do_nothing` records — increments match_count and fires UPDATE statements during validation; stats are inflated and validation becomes a side-effectful DB write path, which also makes should_block? unsafe to call in contexts where writes are not expected.

[ADVISORY] The client adds the email to rejectedEmails for ANY error on the email attribute (including whitelist/blacklist 'not_allowed' and format errors), then displays the generic 'user.email.invalid' message, conflating every email failure with a permanent block. A user whose address was rejected because of the email_domains_whitelist gets a misleading generic 'invalid' message and their address is permanently rejected for the rest of the modal session even if the site setting was the actual (fixable) cause — the client-side scope exceeds the PR's stated intent of handling blocked emails.

[ADVISORY] The new error payload leaks `user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")` back to the client, while the client only consumes result.values.email — name and username in the payload are untraceable to any requirement in this PR. Unnecessary PII/attribute exposure on a public, unauthenticated account-creation endpoint expands the API surface beyond what the client uses; anyone hitting POST /users without a CSRF-valid form can harvest reflected user attributes for free.

[ADVISORY] Moving the domain whitelist/blacklist logic from the removed private email_validator into lib/validators/email_validator.rb is refactoring work only loosely traceable to the stated intent (blocked-user validation) and it changes behavior: the `email: true` validator is gated on email_changed?, so an existing user whose saved email was captured under an old setting configuration is never re-checked. The refactor smuggled into a feature PR means a revert of the blocked-email feature also reverts the validator restructuring (and vice versa), and reviewers cannot evaluate the two independently; the existing-user-never-rechecked gap is a behavior change no test in the diff covers.

[BUG] The new `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` wires the BlockedEmail check to the email_changed? guard, so a user whose email is not changing never hits the blocked-email check. Any code path that creates or updates a User with an unchanged email (e.g., omniauth-provisioned users, invites, admin edits, or any record where email_changed? is false) silently bypasses the blocked-email enforcement the PR's title promises, letting blocked emails through — the objective 'comprehensive email validation for blocked users' only holds on the one controller path this diff touches.

[ADVISORY] should_block? performs a non-idempotent write (match_count += 1, last_match_at, save) inside a model-validation path. Calling `valid?` twice (common in controllers that validate before save, or on retried submits) double-increments match_count and fires extra UPDATEs, corrupting the 'has this email ever been blocked' statistics that last_match_at/match_count exist to provide; operators relying on those stats get wrong counts.

[ADVISORY] BlockedEmail is a ships-inert feature: the diff adds the model and migration but no writer path anywhere (no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, or seed) inserts rows with action_type block. Operators deploy this and nothing blocks anything until someone hand-writes SQL; the 'comprehensive email validation for blocked users' intent cannot be exercised by any supported interface.

[BUG] The first spec ('doesn't add an error when email doesn't match a blocked email') asserts a blank error only under stubbed should_block? and fails to account for the SiteSetting whitelist/blacklist branches in validate_each that run first. If email_domains_blacklist/whitelist settings are set (as other specs in the suite do), the domain regex branches add an error and this spec fails; conversely no spec covers the whitelist/blacklist logic at all, so a regression in the migrated email_in_restriction_setting? code would break signup for every site using those settings with no test catching it.

[BUG] The migration declares action_type as null: false with no database default, relying on the model's before_validation callback to populate it. Any row inserted outside the model (raw SQL, the 'manually load the table' workflow the spec comments explicitly describe, or restore/import tools) raises a NOT NULL violation instead of defaulting to block — the exact operator workflow the PR comment says it supports.

[ADVISORY] The new errors/values payload in the failed-create branch is behavior-bearing public API with no controller spec covering it. The frontend contract (result.errors.email and result.values.email gating rejectedEmails) is untested; a refactor renaming the error key silently disables the client-side rejected-email feedback with no failing test.

[ADVISORY] The rejectedEmails check runs before the authOptions check, and rejectedEmails is never cleared when the modal is reopened. A user whose auth-provided email (e.g., Twitter/Facebook) was rejected once sees 'user.email.invalid' for that address on every subsequent signup attempt in the same session even if the block was lifted server-side, with no way to clear the client state short of a page reload.

[BUG] The whitelist/blacklist domain regex is unanchored and matches the domain substring anywhere after '@', so a whitelist of 'discourse.org' accepts 'user@discourse.org.evil.com' and a blacklist entry is trivially evaded by an attacker whose domain merely contains the blocked string as a prefix. An attacker registers with an email at a domain that embeds a whitelisted domain as a prefix (e.g. discourse.org.attacker.com), passing email_domains_whitelist and signing up from a provider the site admin explicitly tried to exclude; likewise blacklisted providers get signups through via 'spamclub.com.mydomain.org'.

[BUG] The admin-configured email_domains_whitelist/blacklist value is interpolated into Regexp.new with only dots escaped, so any regex metacharacter a site admin places in the setting (parens, brackets, alternation, quantifiers) is executed as regex syntax — an injection sink fed from the config store. An admin who enters a comma- or newline-separated domain list (the natural expectation for a 'domains' setting) silently produces a regex that never matches or matches everything: a blacklist entry like 'a.com, b.com' compiles with ', b.com' as literal-ish junk and the control fails open/closed unpredictably; a crafted alternation can also produce catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS) on every signup attempt, since the pattern is evaluated against attacker-supplied email strings.

[ADVISORY] BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact, case-sensitive `where(email: email)` lookup with no downcasing or normalization, so a blocked address stored in any non-lowercase form ('Spam@x.com') is bypassed by supplying the lowercase variant, and vice versa. A moderator who loads the blocked_emails table with mixed-case addresses (the standard way to seed this table, per the spec's own comment about manual loading) gets a control that silently fails to block the same address typed in a different case; blocked users get through and the match_count/last_match_at audit trail stays empty, hiding the bypass.

[ADVISORY] The validator triggers a persistent write (BlockedEmail.should_block? increments match_count and saves) as a side effect of model validation, so a write occurs every time any record with a changed email is validated, including during unrelated flows, and the record.save inside should_block? can itself fail validation (email uniqueness/presence) raising an exception inside the signup path. Any code path that validates a user (including failed signup attempts, which are unauthenticated and repeatable) causes a DB write per attempt, giving an anonymous attacker a cheap write-amplification vector against the blocked_emails table; and a save failure inside should_block? surfaces as a 500 on account creation instead of the validation error the contract promises.

[ADVISORY] The new EmailValidator spec covers only the BlockedEmail branch and never triggers the whitelist or blacklist branches of validate_each, even though this diff moved that restriction logic out of user.rb's email_validator and into validate_each. The whitelist/blacklist regex logic (email_in_restriction_setting?, including the escaping of '.' and the case-insensitive Regexp) ships with zero test coverage in this diff; a regression in domain restriction (e.g. breaking the gsub escape so 'example.com' matches 'examplexcom') silently lets users register from blacklisted domains, and no spec in the diff catches it. I checked spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb and spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb — neither references email_domains_whitelist, email_domains_blacklist, or email_in_restriction_setting?.

[ADVISORY] Both specs stub BlockedEmail.should_block?, so the validator's real guard 'if record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)' is never exercised with a pre-populated error, and the interaction between the restriction branch and the blocked branch is untested. If the guard is ever removed or reordered, a user with a whitelisted-domain violation plus a blocked email would get a confusing doubled error (or, inverted, a blacklisted email would skip the blocked check entirely); the existing specs pass in every one of those mutations because the stub guarantees should_block? returns exactly what the assertion assumes — a mirror test asserting the stub, not the code. I checked both new spec files; no context sets SiteSetting restrictions together with should_block?.

[ADVISORY] The negative-path spec asserts only record.errors[:email].should_not be_present without verifying the stubbed should_block? was actually consulted, so a mutation deleting the BlockedEmail branch from EmailValidator entirely still passes this test. A future refactor that drops the blocked-email check loses its only supposed safety net — the 'doesn't add an error' spec passes identically with and without the BlockedEmail code, giving false confidence that blocked-email behavior is regression-covered at the validator level.

[ADVISORY] The should_block? specs exercise a read path whose only real-world caller is inside a validation, so the side-effect-in-validator hazard (should_block? does record.save on every user validation attempt, incrementing match_count even when validation ultimately fails or the email is only typed, never submitted) has no spec pinning the intended semantics. Anyone changing should_block? to fire on partial-email keystrokes or repeated failed submissions (multi-counting) has no spec distinguishing 'count one per validation attempt' from 'count one per blocked attempt'; I checked spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb — it asserts the current side effect (change match_count by 1 per call) but no spec ties the call frequency to a validation event, so the counter's business meaning is unpinned.

[BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact case-sensitive string match (`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`) against an un-normalized email column, so a block on "spammer@evil.com" is bypassed by registering "Spammer@evil.com" or "SPAMMER@EVIL.com". An attacker evades the blocklist by varying letter case; the migration (20130724201552) creates the column with no downcasing/normalization and the unique index is on the raw string, so operators loading the table with mixed-case emails get duplicate rows for the same address, one of which blocks and one of which doesn't.

[ADVISORY] EmailValidator runs BlockedEmail.should_block?, which writes to the database (increments match_count and sets last_match_at) inside the User validation pass. Statistics are incremented on every validation attempt — failed creates, retries, and even validations that later fail for other reasons (e.g. password) all count as "matches", so last_match_at/match_count misreport real blocking activity; admins using these columns (per the model spec's stated purpose of seeing whether a loaded email was ever blocked) get inflated data.

[ADVISORY] should_block? uses a read-modify-write on match_count (`record.match_count += 1` then `record.save`) instead of an atomic `update_counters`/SQL increment. Concurrent signup attempts for the same blocked email lose counter increments (two processes read match_count=5, both write 6), and the full `record.save` also re-runs BlockedEmail validations on every user-create request — a hot-path extra write on the signup path with the counter drift as the observable defect.

[ADVISORY] The controller pushes the email into rejectedEmails on ANY email-keyed server error, including non-permanent errors like "email already taken" (the uniqueness validation the same diff keeps on User.email), and the email validation then permanently rejects that address with the "user.email.invalid" message until the modal is reloaded. A user whose email collides with an existing account is told the email is invalid and cannot retry with the same (legitimate) address in that session — the client-side block fires before the request even reaches the server again, so the real error message (already taken vs blocked) is masked.

[BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? looks up `where(email: email)` with a case-sensitive string comparison, so a registration using any case variant of a blocked address bypasses the block entirely. A user (or spammer) whose address is in blocked_emails registers successfully as 'BLOCK@SpamFromHome.org' or 'Block@Spamfromhome.org'; should_block? returns false, no block error, and the entire feature is defeated by capitalizing one letter.

[BUG] The validation path mutates and saves a different model (BlockedEmail#save inside should_block?) from within validate_each, so a failure of that write raises an unhandled ActiveRecord error during validation. If the BlockedEmail save fails (unique-index race on concurrent registration attempts, stale read-modify-write on match_count, or a validation failure on that row), the exception propagates out of user.save and the users#create rescue only catches StatementInvalid, turning a routine duplicate-signup into a 500 instead of the 4xx JSON error the endpoint returns elsewhere.

[BUG] should_block? uses read-then-write (fetch, match_count += 1, save) with no lock, so concurrent signups for the same blocked email lose counter increments. match_count and last_match_at under-report actual block hits for the admin who loaded the table to observe blocking frequency; under concurrent spam bursts the statistics this feature exists to produce are silently wrong.

[ADVISORY] The client-side rejectedEmails check reports the failure with I18n.t('user.email.invalid') instead of the blocked-email message, while the server reports 'is not allowed.' A user whose email was blocked sees 'invalid' on subsequent keystrokes but a different message on submit — the inline hint misdirects them toward fixing a malformed address rather than using another one; misleading-error-content on the primary user-facing path of this feature.

[ADVISORY] rejectedEmails matching is an exact string comparison against result.values.email, so any retyped case variant or whitespace difference never matches the stored rejection and the client-side block never fires. A user blocked on 'bad@x.com' who edits the field to 'Bad@x.com' bypasses the inline validation, submits again, and burns a full server round-trip that re-rejects and pushes the new variant — a silent client/server desync where the added client validation is ineffective for exactly the input variations users produce.

The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, the guard is `if record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`. `record.errors[attribute]` is the model’s accumulated errors for that attribute, not just errors added by the earlier whitelist/blacklist branch in this validator. Since `User` declares `validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true` before `validates :email, email: true`, presence/uniqueness errors would already populate `record.errors[:email]`, causing the guard to be false and preventing both the blocked error from being appended and `BlockedEmail.should_block?` from being called/mutating rows.

Concurrent signups for the same blocked email (e.g. a spam bot firing parallel requests) lose increments, and a validation failure in BlockedEmail's own before_validation/uniqueness check silently drops the stats write with no log — the caller never learns the counter update failed.

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?` the diff shows a non-atomic read/modify/write counter update: `record.match_count += 1; record.last_match_at = ...; record.save` (app/models/blocked_email.rb). Under concurrent calls for the same `blocked_emails` row, increments can be lost because there is no locking or atomic `UPDATE ... SET match_count = match_count + 1`. The code also ignores `record.save`’s return value, so a failed save would silently drop the stats update. (The finding’s mention of uniqueness/before_validation failure is speculative, but the concurrency/ignored-save issues are directly grounded in the diff.)

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, any server-side email error causes `result.values.email` to be pushed into the persistent controller property `rejectedEmails` (`if (result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values) ... pushObject(...)`). Subsequent validation short-circuits on `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` and returns a failure with the generic `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`, discarding the server’s specific reason (e.g. `user.email.blocked` / `user.email.not_allowed` / uniqueness). The diff shows no code clearing `rejectedEmails` when the modal closes or the form resets, so within the lifetime of the Ember app/controller the user can be permanently blocked from retrying the same email even if the underlying condition changes, and they will see an incorrect reason string.

adjudication.rationale: In create_account_controller.js, on failed signup it unconditionally caches the attempted email in `rejectedEmails` whenever `result.errors.email` exists (`pushObject(result.values.email)`), without checking which validation failed. Later, `emailValidation` treats any cached email as invalid and returns a generic `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`. On the server, email failures can be `user.email.not_allowed` (whitelist/blacklist), `user.email.blocked`, uniqueness, etc. (users_controller now returns `errors: user.errors.to_hash`). This means non-blocked/temporary errors (e.g., duplicate, domain not allowed) become locally “permanently” rejected for the modal session and the client shows a different message than the server would provide.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] email_in_restriction_setting? builds an unescaped alternation regexp from raw site-setting text via Regexp.new, so entries containing regex metacharacters (a domain typo like 'foo|bar' or '(' in the admin-entered list) raise RegexpError at validation time. A site admin entering a malformed domain list turns every account creation and every email update into a 500 for all users until the setting is reverted; this flaw was merely moved verbatim from the deleted User#email_validator rather than fixed during extraction.

adjudication.rationale: In lib/validators/email_validator.rb, email_in_restriction_setting? interpolates the raw SiteSetting string into Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true) after only gsub-ing '.' -> '\\.'. Any other regex metacharacters in the admin-entered whitelist/blacklist (e.g., '(', ')', '[', '|' etc.) can change regex meaning or raise RegexpError (e.g., unbalanced parentheses) during validation, potentially causing 500s on account creation/email update. The diff shows this logic was moved verbatim from the removed User#email_in_restriction_setting? without additional escaping/guarding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] BlockedEmail has no writer anywhere in this diff — no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, seed, or data-entry path creates blocked_emails records — so the feature ships inert. Operators cannot actually block an email without hand-written SQL; the entire BlockedEmail table, validator branch, and client-side rejectedEmails mechanism are dead weight until someone adds an entry path, and no acceptance criterion in the diff verifies the end-to-end block of a real email.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a `blocked_emails` table, `BlockedEmail` model, and an `EmailValidator` branch that calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`, plus client-side `rejectedEmails` handling. However, within this diff there is no admin UI/controller/API/rake task/seed or other runtime path that creates `BlockedEmail` rows (creation appears only in specs/fabricators). As a result, in normal operation the blocklist will remain empty unless operators manually insert records, making the new blocking feature effectively unusable until an entry mechanism is added. This is an incompleteness/scope issue rather than a directly verifiable correctness bug in the shown code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The client adds the submitted email to rejectedEmails for any server-side email error, not only a 'blocked' error, so an email rejected for 'has already been taken' is permanently shown as 'user.email.invalid'. A user whose email collides with an existing account retries that same address later (e.g., after the original account is deleted) and the client still refuses it with the generic invalid-email message, plus no client-side test in the diff covers the pushObject branch at all.

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, any failed create response with `result.errors.email` causes `rejectedEmails.pushObject(result.values.email)` (no check for a specific error like `user.email.blocked`). Later, `emailValidation` unconditionally fails if `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` and reports `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`, preventing resubmission of that same email within the controller’s lifetime even if the original server-side error was something else (e.g., uniqueness). This behavior is directly introduced by the new `rejectedEmails` logic and can misclassify/lock out an email address client-side.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new EmailValidator's whitelist and blacklist branches (lib/validators/email_validator.rb lines 6-11) have zero spec coverage — every test in the new spec stubs should_block? and runs with SiteSettings unset, so `email_in_restriction_setting?` and the regexp gsub/escape logic copied from user.rb are never executed. A regression in the migrated domain-restriction logic (e.g., the dot-escaping or case-insensitive regexp construction) would pass the entire suite while breaking whitelist/blacklist signup for every site using those settings.

adjudication.rationale: The new spec (spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb) only exercises the BlockedEmail.should_block? path by stubbing it and does not set SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist or SiteSetting.email_domains_blacklist. Therefore the whitelist/blacklist branches and the email_in_restriction_setting? regexp/gsub logic in lib/validators/email_validator.rb (lines 6-20 in the added file) are never executed by these tests, so regressions in the migrated domain-restriction logic could slip through. This is a concrete, diff-grounded test coverage gap rather than a proven runtime defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a write (`record.save`) inside a User validation read-path, so two concurrent signups with the same blocked email race on match_count (lost update) and the save failure is silently ignored because the return value is never checked. Operators inspecting match_count/last_match_at to judge whether a blocked email is being abused get undercounted statistics, and any save failure (uniqueness race, validation drift) silently drops the stats update while the block decision still proceeds.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `EmailValidator` which calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` during user email validation (`validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`). `BlockedEmail.should_block?` performs a read-modify-write (`record.match_count += 1; record.last_match_at = Time.zone.now; record.save`) without any locking/atomic update, so concurrent validations for the same blocked email can lose increments. Also, `record.save`'s return value is ignored and failures would not be surfaced, while the block decision still proceeds based on `record.action_type`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new errors/values payload is emitted only on the validation-failure branch and has no spec anywhere in the diff (no UsersController create spec, no client test asserting the rejectedEmails push), so the server contract the JS at create_account_controller.js:274-276 depends on is completely unverified. The exact shape `result.errors.email && result.values.email` is untested in both directions — a serialization change (e.g., symbol keys, attribute renaming) would silently disable the client-side rejected-email UX with no failing test.

adjudication.rationale: In `UsersController#create`, the diff adds `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")` only on the failure JSON branch. The Ember client change in `create_account_controller.js` depends on that exact shape (`result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values` then `result.values.email`) to push into `rejectedEmails`. The diff adds specs for `EmailValidator` and `BlockedEmail`, but no controller/request spec verifying the new JSON contract, and no client-side test asserting the rejectedEmails behavior. This makes the new server-client contract brittle and unverified, but it’s not a demonstrable runtime bug from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The BlockedEmail check inherits the `if: :email_changed?` gate, so updating any other attribute on a persisted user whose email already lives in blocked_emails passes validation — but the diff also drops the old email_validator's unconditional coverage question without any spec confirming email_changed? is true on User.create. If email_changed? is false on any creation path (e.g., an assignment path that bypasses change tracking in this Rails version), a blocked email sails through signup with no test in the diff to catch it, since the validator spec builds a bare record and calls validate_each directly rather than through User.create.

adjudication.rationale: In user.rb the new custom validator is only invoked via `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`, so the BlockedEmail check will not run when updating a persisted user unless the email attribute changes. Also, the added specs exercise `EmailValidator#validate_each` directly and do not cover the integration path (e.g., `User.create` / full-model validation) where the `if: :email_changed?` gate could affect whether the validator runs. The finding’s broader claim that create may bypass change tracking is speculative from the diff alone, but the gating + lack of an integration spec is diff-grounded.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Blocked-email enforcement runs only `if: :email_changed?`, but the whole point of the feature is to stop blocked users, and BlockedEmail.should_block? matches the stored email with an exact case-sensitive string comparison, so the check is bypassable. A user whose email was added to blocked_emails re-registers with mixed-case or trailing-variant of the same address (BlockedEmail.where(email: email) in blocked_email.rb finds no row because the lookup is not downcased/normalized), defeats the block, and the invariant the PR claims to enforce — blocked users cannot create accounts — silently fails.

[ADVISORY] The blocked_emails table and BlockedEmail model ship with no writer anywhere in the diff — no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, seed, or staff controller ever creates a BlockedEmail row. Site operators who deploy this PR have no way to actually block an email address; the feature is inert until a follow-up admin interface lands, and the reviewer cannot trace the end-to-end requirement to any usable path.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `blocked_emails` (migration) plus `BlockedEmail` and wires it into `EmailValidator` (`BlockedEmail.should_block?`). Within the shown changes, there is no UI/controller/admin/API/rake/seed code added to create or manage `BlockedEmail` rows—only the read/check path exists. However, the claim that operators have *no way* to populate it cannot be fully verified from this diff alone, since such a writer could already exist elsewhere in the codebase (outside the provided patch).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] BlockedEmail.should_block? performs a read-modify-write (record.match_count += 1; record.save) inside an ActiveModel validation, so merely validating a user mutates blocked_emails rows. Every validation pass — including retries, failed saves for unrelated reasons, and `do_nothing` records — increments match_count and fires UPDATE statements during validation; stats are inflated and validation becomes a side-effectful DB write path, which also makes should_block? unsafe to call in contexts where writes are not expected.
matched_golden_ids: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both point out that the `should_block...` method is not a pure check: it performs a read-modify-write by incrementing `match_count` and saving, so calling it (e.g., during validation) mutates DB state and inflates stats. This matches the golden concern about side effects during a read/check operation making the method misleading and problematic in concurrent/"read-only" contexts.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The client adds the email to rejectedEmails for ANY error on the email attribute (including whitelist/blacklist 'not_allowed' and format errors), then displays the generic 'user.email.invalid' message, conflating every email failure with a permanent block. A user whose address was rejected because of the email_domains_whitelist gets a misleading generic 'invalid' message and their address is permanently rejected for the rest of the modal session even if the site setting was the actual (fixable) cause — the client-side scope exceeds the PR's stated intent of handling blocked emails.

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, any server-side error on `email` triggers `rejectedEmails.pushObject(result.values.email)` (guard only checks `result.errors.email`, not the specific error) in the failure branch of the create call. Later, `emailMatch` short-circuits if `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` and returns `failed: true` with the generic `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`, regardless of whether the server error was `user.email.not_allowed`, `user.email.blocked`, uniqueness, etc. This both misreports the reason and makes that exact email fail client-side for the rest of the modal session, even if the underlying server-side condition changes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new error payload leaks `user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")` back to the client, while the client only consumes result.values.email — name and username in the payload are untraceable to any requirement in this PR. Unnecessary PII/attribute exposure on a public, unauthenticated account-creation endpoint expands the API surface beyond what the client uses; anyone hitting POST /users without a CSRF-valid form can harvest reflected user attributes for free.

adjudication.rationale: In `UsersController#create`, the failure JSON response was expanded to include `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")` (and `errors: user.errors.to_hash`). In the client change (`create_account_controller.js`), only `result.values.email` is used to populate `rejectedEmails`. The extra `name` and `username` fields are therefore unnecessary API surface for this PR and could reasonably be trimmed to just what the client needs. However, the diff only shows echoing back user-submitted attributes (not leaking server-side private data), so framing it as a concrete security defect/PII leak is not fully supported by the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Moving the domain whitelist/blacklist logic from the removed private email_validator into lib/validators/email_validator.rb is refactoring work only loosely traceable to the stated intent (blocked-user validation) and it changes behavior: the `email: true` validator is gated on email_changed?, so an existing user whose saved email was captured under an old setting configuration is never re-checked. The refactor smuggled into a feature PR means a revert of the blocked-email feature also reverts the validator restructuring (and vice versa), and reviewers cannot evaluate the two independently; the existing-user-never-rechecked gap is a behavior change no test in the diff covers.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does bundle a structural refactor (moving the domain whitelist/blacklist logic out of `User#email_validator` into a new `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, and changing `User` to `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`) together with the new blocked-email feature (`BlockedEmail` + `BlockedEmail.should_block?`). That coupling means reverting the blocked-email feature would also revert the validator restructuring, making the changes harder to review/rollback independently. However, the claimed behavior change about gating on `email_changed?` is not supported by the diff: the removed callback was also guarded by `if: :email_changed?` (`validate :email_validator, if: :email_changed?`), so “existing user emails are never re-checked” is not newly introduced here. The new specs focus on blocked-email behavior and don’t cover whitelist/blacklist behavior after the move.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The new `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` wires the BlockedEmail check to the email_changed? guard, so a user whose email is not changing never hits the blocked-email check. Any code path that creates or updates a User with an unchanged email (e.g., omniauth-provisioned users, invites, admin edits, or any record where email_changed? is false) silently bypasses the blocked-email enforcement the PR's title promises, letting blocked emails through — the objective 'comprehensive email validation for blocked users' only holds on the one controller path this diff touches.

adjudication.rationale: In `app/models/user.rb` the new validator is wired as `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`, and the blocked-email enforcement lives inside `EmailValidator#validate_each` (`BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`). Therefore the blocked-email check only runs when `email_changed?` is true; saves/updates that don’t modify `email` will not re-check against `blocked_emails`. However, this is not clearly a defect introduced by the diff because the previous implementation also gated email-domain validation behind `if: :email_changed?` (`validate :email_validator, if: :email_changed?`). The finding’s claim that “creates ... with an unchanged email ... bypasses” isn’t directly verifiable from the diff (new records typically have `email_changed?` true), but the scope/architecture concern about when the new blocked-email policy is enforced is real and diff-grounded.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] should_block? performs a non-idempotent write (match_count += 1, last_match_at, save) inside a model-validation path. Calling `valid?` twice (common in controllers that validate before save, or on retried submits) double-increments match_count and fires extra UPDATEs, corrupting the 'has this email ever been blocked' statistics that last_match_at/match_count exist to provide; operators relying on those stats get wrong counts.

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, the validator calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` when validating a User's email (via `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`). `BlockedEmail.should_block?` (new in `app/models/blocked_email.rb`) performs writes (`match_count += 1`, `last_match_at = ...`, `save`) every time it is called. Since validations can be invoked multiple times (e.g., repeated `valid?` calls, retries, or multiple validation passes before/around persistence), this will double-increment `match_count` and update `last_match_at` multiple times for the same attempted signup, producing incorrect statistics and extra UPDATEs during validation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] BlockedEmail is a ships-inert feature: the diff adds the model and migration but no writer path anywhere (no admin UI, API endpoint, rake task, or seed) inserts rows with action_type block. Operators deploy this and nothing blocks anything until someone hand-writes SQL; the 'comprehensive email validation for blocked users' intent cannot be exercised by any supported interface.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `BlockedEmail` (model + migration) and wires it into validation via the new `EmailValidator` (`BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)`), but within this PR there is no code path added that creates/populates `blocked_emails` records in normal operation (no controller/admin endpoint/seed/rake task). Aside from tests/fabricators, nothing in the shown changes writes to `blocked_emails`, so the blocking behavior will be effectively unused unless rows are added out-of-band.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The first spec ('doesn't add an error when email doesn't match a blocked email') asserts a blank error only under stubbed should_block? and fails to account for the SiteSetting whitelist/blacklist branches in validate_each that run first. If email_domains_blacklist/whitelist settings are set (as other specs in the suite do), the domain regex branches add an error and this spec fails; conversely no spec covers the whitelist/blacklist logic at all, so a regression in the migrated email_in_restriction_setting? code would break signup for every site using those settings with no test catching it.

adjudication.rationale: In `EmailValidator#validate_each`, the whitelist/blacklist branches run before the `BlockedEmail.should_block?` check (lib/validators/email_validator.rb). But the spec `"doesn't add an error when email doesn't match a blocked email"` only stubs `BlockedEmail.should_block?` and then asserts `record.errors[:email]` is blank (spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb); it does not ensure `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist/blacklist` are blank, so the test is not isolated from those settings and could fail if they are set elsewhere in the suite. Also, the diff adds/migrates nontrivial whitelist/blacklist logic into this validator without any dedicated specs covering those branches, so regressions in `email_in_restriction_setting?` or branching behavior would not be caught by tests in this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The migration declares action_type as null: false with no database default, relying on the model's before_validation callback to populate it. Any row inserted outside the model (raw SQL, the 'manually load the table' workflow the spec comments explicitly describe, or restore/import tools) raises a NOT NULL violation instead of defaulting to block — the exact operator workflow the PR comment says it supports.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb` defines `action_type` as `null: false` with no DB default, while `BlockedEmail` sets a default via `before_validation :set_defaults` (`self.action_type ||= ...`). That means inserts that bypass the model (raw SQL/import tools) must provide `action_type` or they will hit a NOT NULL violation, so the schema isn’t robust to out-of-band inserts. However, this does not break normal app behavior shown in the diff (Rails model creation will populate it), so it’s more an operational/schema-design issue than an in-app correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new errors/values payload in the failed-create branch is behavior-bearing public API with no controller spec covering it. The frontend contract (result.errors.email and result.values.email gating rejectedEmails) is untested; a refactor renaming the error key silently disables the client-side rejected-email feedback with no failing test.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new behavior-bearing JSON fields in UsersController#create failure response (`errors: user.errors.to_hash`, `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")`) and the frontend now conditionally uses them to populate `rejectedEmails` (`if (result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values) { ... pushObject(result.values.email) }`). The diff includes model/validator specs but no controller/request spec asserting the failed-create payload shape or that `errors.email`/`values.email` are present, so a backend refactor changing keys could silently break this new client-side feedback without a failing test.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The rejectedEmails check runs before the authOptions check, and rejectedEmails is never cleared when the modal is reopened. A user whose auth-provided email (e.g., Twitter/Facebook) was rejected once sees 'user.email.invalid' for that address on every subsequent signup attempt in the same session even if the block was lifted server-side, with no way to clear the client state short of a page reload.

adjudication.rationale: In `create_account_controller.js`, `emailValidation` now short-circuits on `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` *before* the `authOptions.email`/`authOptions.email_valid` fast-path (added block around lines ~65-76 vs existing authOptions check right after). Additionally, the only mutation shown is `pushObject(result.values.email)` on a failed create (lines ~271-274), and there is no code in the diff that ever removes entries from `rejectedEmails` or resets it. That means once an email is added to `rejectedEmails`, the client will keep returning `failed: true` for that same email regardless of later server-side acceptability, and it will also override an `authOptions.email_valid` email because the rejectedEmails check runs first.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The whitelist/blacklist domain regex is unanchored and matches the domain substring anywhere after '@', so a whitelist of 'discourse.org' accepts 'user@discourse.org.evil.com' and a blacklist entry is trivially evaded by an attacker whose domain merely contains the blocked string as a prefix. An attacker registers with an email at a domain that embeds a whitelisted domain as a prefix (e.g. discourse.org.attacker.com), passing email_domains_whitelist and signing up from a provider the site admin explicitly tried to exclude; likewise blacklisted providers get signups through via 'spamclub.com.mydomain.org'.
matched_golden_ids: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both comments identify the same underlying flaw: the email domain whitelist/blacklist regex is not properly boundary-anchored, so it can match a whitelisted/blacklisted domain as a substring within a longer attacker-controlled domain (e.g., discourse.org.evil.com / evil.example.com), enabling bypass or evasion.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The admin-configured email_domains_whitelist/blacklist value is interpolated into Regexp.new with only dots escaped, so any regex metacharacter a site admin places in the setting (parens, brackets, alternation, quantifiers) is executed as regex syntax — an injection sink fed from the config store. An admin who enters a comma- or newline-separated domain list (the natural expectation for a 'domains' setting) silently produces a regex that never matches or matches everything: a blacklist entry like 'a.com, b.com' compiles with ', b.com' as literal-ish junk and the control fails open/closed unpredictably; a crafted alternation can also produce catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS) on every signup attempt, since the pattern is evaluated against attacker-supplied email strings.

adjudication.rationale: In lib/validators/email_validator.rb, email_in_restriction_setting? builds a regex via `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)` where `domains` is derived from the admin setting with only `.` escaped (`setting.gsub('.', '\\.')`). Any other regex metacharacters in the setting (e.g., `()[]|+*?`) will be interpreted as regex syntax, and comma/newline-separated "lists" will be treated literally rather than as separate domains. This can cause whitelist/blacklist checks to fail open/closed unexpectedly and can enable pathological regex patterns (potential ReDoS) evaluated against user-supplied email values on signup.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact, case-sensitive `where(email: email)` lookup with no downcasing or normalization, so a blocked address stored in any non-lowercase form ('Spam@x.com') is bypassed by supplying the lowercase variant, and vice versa. A moderator who loads the blocked_emails table with mixed-case addresses (the standard way to seed this table, per the spec's own comment about manual loading) gets a control that silently fails to block the same address typed in a different case; blocked users get through and the match_count/last_match_at audit trail stays empty, hiding the bypass.
matched_golden_ids: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both the golden and candidate describe the same flaw: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` performs a case-sensitive email lookup without normalization, allowing a blocked email to bypass the check by changing letter case (e.g., User@Example.com vs user@example.com), resulting in blocked users getting through.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The validator triggers a persistent write (BlockedEmail.should_block? increments match_count and saves) as a side effect of model validation, so a write occurs every time any record with a changed email is validated, including during unrelated flows, and the record.save inside should_block? can itself fail validation (email uniqueness/presence) raising an exception inside the signup path. Any code path that validates a user (including failed signup attempts, which are unauthenticated and repeatable) causes a DB write per attempt, giving an anonymous attacker a cheap write-amplification vector against the blocked_emails table; and a save failure inside should_block? surfaces as a 500 on account creation instead of the validation error the contract promises.

adjudication.rationale: The diff makes `User` email validation call the new `EmailValidator` (`validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`), and `EmailValidator#validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` when no prior email-domain errors exist. `BlockedEmail.should_block?` updates `match_count`/`last_match_at` and executes `record.save`, so validating a user with a blocked email causes a DB write as a side effect of validation (including unauthenticated, repeatable signup attempts), which is a real write-amplification/DoS-style risk. The finding’s claim that this will “raise an exception” on save failure is not shown by the diff because it uses `save` (not `save!`), but the side-effectful write during validation is directly verifiable.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new EmailValidator spec covers only the BlockedEmail branch and never triggers the whitelist or blacklist branches of validate_each, even though this diff moved that restriction logic out of user.rb's email_validator and into validate_each. The whitelist/blacklist regex logic (email_in_restriction_setting?, including the escaping of '.' and the case-insensitive Regexp) ships with zero test coverage in this diff; a regression in domain restriction (e.g. breaking the gsub escape so 'example.com' matches 'examplexcom') silently lets users register from blacklisted domains, and no spec in the diff catches it. I checked spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb and spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb — neither references email_domains_whitelist, email_domains_blacklist, or email_in_restriction_setting?.

adjudication.rationale: The diff moves the domain whitelist/blacklist restriction logic out of `User#email_validator` (removed from `app/models/user.rb`) into the new `lib/validators/email_validator.rb` (`validate_each` + `email_in_restriction_setting?`). The added spec `spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb` only stubs and asserts behavior around `BlockedEmail.should_block?` and never sets/uses `SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist` or `SiteSetting.email_domains_blacklist`, nor does it exercise the regex logic (`setting.gsub('.', '\.')` and `Regexp.new(..., true)`). So this is a concrete, diff-grounded missing-test issue for newly relocated nontrivial validation behavior, not a proven runtime defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Both specs stub BlockedEmail.should_block?, so the validator's real guard 'if record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)' is never exercised with a pre-populated error, and the interaction between the restriction branch and the blocked branch is untested. If the guard is ever removed or reordered, a user with a whitelisted-domain violation plus a blocked email would get a confusing doubled error (or, inverted, a blacklisted email would skip the blocked check entirely); the existing specs pass in every one of those mutations because the stub guarantees should_block? returns exactly what the assertion assumes — a mirror test asserting the stub, not the code. I checked both new spec files; no context sets SiteSetting restrictions together with should_block?.

adjudication.rationale: In `spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb`, both examples stub `BlockedEmail.should_block?` and never set up a scenario where the earlier whitelist/blacklist branches add an `:email` error before the `if record.errors[attribute].blank? and BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` guard runs. As a result, the interaction/precedence between the restriction errors and the blocked-email error (i.e., ensuring blocked checks are skipped when an email restriction error already exists, and that no double-error occurs) is untested. This is a concrete, diff-grounded test gap in the newly added validator logic, not a demonstrable runtime defect in the diff itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The negative-path spec asserts only record.errors[:email].should_not be_present without verifying the stubbed should_block? was actually consulted, so a mutation deleting the BlockedEmail branch from EmailValidator entirely still passes this test. A future refactor that drops the blocked-email check loses its only supposed safety net — the 'doesn't add an error' spec passes identically with and without the BlockedEmail code, giving false confidence that blocked-email behavior is regression-covered at the validator level.

adjudication.rationale: In spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb, the “doesn't add an error when email doesn't match a blocked email” example stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? to return false but only asserts record.errors[:email].should_not be_present; it does not assert BlockedEmail.should_block? was actually invoked. If the BlockedEmail check in lib/validators/email_validator.rb were removed entirely, this negative-path test would still pass (since no error would be added), reducing its value as regression coverage for the newly added blocked-email logic. This is a test robustness issue, not a functional defect in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The should_block? specs exercise a read path whose only real-world caller is inside a validation, so the side-effect-in-validator hazard (should_block? does record.save on every user validation attempt, incrementing match_count even when validation ultimately fails or the email is only typed, never submitted) has no spec pinning the intended semantics. Anyone changing should_block? to fire on partial-email keystrokes or repeated failed submissions (multi-counting) has no spec distinguishing 'count one per validation attempt' from 'count one per blocked attempt'; I checked spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb — it asserts the current side effect (change match_count by 1 per call) but no spec ties the call frequency to a validation event, so the counter's business meaning is unpinned.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a side-effectful path in validation: `EmailValidator#validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` and, if a record exists, `should_block?` increments `match_count`, sets `last_match_at`, and `save`s (app/models/blocked_email.rb, lib/validators/email_validator.rb). The existing spec (spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb) pins only that each *call* increments the counter by 1, but there is no spec tying when/how often `should_block?` is invoked in real flows (e.g., repeated validations during a single failed signup). That leaves the intended business meaning of `match_count` (per validation vs per blocked signup attempt) unpinned, as the finding describes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact case-sensitive string match (`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first`) against an un-normalized email column, so a block on "spammer@evil.com" is bypassed by registering "Spammer@evil.com" or "SPAMMER@EVIL.com". An attacker evades the blocklist by varying letter case; the migration (20130724201552) creates the column with no downcasing/normalization and the unique index is on the raw string, so operators loading the table with mixed-case emails get duplicate rows for the same address, one of which blocks and one of which doesn't.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `BlockedEmail.should_block?` which looks up records via `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` (exact match) and the migration creates `blocked_emails.email` with a unique index on the raw string, with no normalization/downcasing in the model (`set_defaults` only sets `action_type`). The new `EmailValidator` passes the user-provided `value` directly to `should_block?`. From what’s shown, mixed-case variants of the same email would not match a differently-cased blocked entry and could also produce duplicate rows differing only by case, so the block can be bypassed by case variation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] EmailValidator runs BlockedEmail.should_block?, which writes to the database (increments match_count and sets last_match_at) inside the User validation pass. Statistics are incremented on every validation attempt — failed creates, retries, and even validations that later fail for other reasons (e.g. password) all count as "matches", so last_match_at/match_count misreport real blocking activity; admins using these columns (per the model spec's stated purpose of seeing whether a loaded email was ever blocked) get inflated data.

adjudication.rationale: In `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, validation calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` when there are no prior email errors. `BlockedEmail.should_block?` (new in `app/models/blocked_email.rb`) performs DB writes (`match_count += 1`, `last_match_at = Time.zone.now`, `record.save`) on every validation run where a `blocked_emails` row exists for that email, regardless of whether the overall `User` record ultimately saves successfully. Since validations can run multiple times (failed create attempts, retries, or later failing due to other attributes like password), this inflates `match_count` and updates `last_match_at`, misrepresenting actual blocking activity as described in the model spec comment about using `last_match_at` to see whether an email "have ever been blocked".

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] should_block? uses a read-modify-write on match_count (`record.match_count += 1` then `record.save`) instead of an atomic `update_counters`/SQL increment. Concurrent signup attempts for the same blocked email lose counter increments (two processes read match_count=5, both write 6), and the full `record.save` also re-runs BlockedEmail validations on every user-create request — a hot-path extra write on the signup path with the counter drift as the observable defect.

adjudication.rationale: In `app/models/blocked_email.rb`, `BlockedEmail.should_block?` does `record = BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` then `record.match_count += 1; ...; record.save`. This is a classic read-modify-write sequence that is not atomic and can lose increments under concurrent calls for the same `blocked_emails.email` row. The diff clearly introduces this counter/stat update in the signup validation hot path, and `save` will also re-run model callbacks/validations each time.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The controller pushes the email into rejectedEmails on ANY email-keyed server error, including non-permanent errors like "email already taken" (the uniqueness validation the same diff keeps on User.email), and the email validation then permanently rejects that address with the "user.email.invalid" message until the modal is reloaded. A user whose email collides with an existing account is told the email is invalid and cannot retry with the same (legitimate) address in that session — the client-side block fires before the request even reaches the server again, so the real error message (already taken vs blocked) is masked.

adjudication.rationale: In create_account_controller.js, any server failure response that includes `result.errors.email` causes `result.values.email` to be pushed into `rejectedEmails` (`pushObject(result.values.email)`). The email validator then immediately fails client-side for any email in that list (`rejectedEmails.contains(email)`) and returns `I18n.t('user.email.invalid')` before re-contacting the server. Since the diff also keeps `validates :email, ... uniqueness: true` on `User`, a common, non-permanent error like “email has already been taken” will trigger this path, causing the UI to incorrectly treat a legitimate email as “invalid” and preventing retry with the same email for the remainder of the modal session (masking the real server-side error).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] BlockedEmail.should_block? looks up `where(email: email)` with a case-sensitive string comparison, so a registration using any case variant of a blocked address bypasses the block entirely. A user (or spammer) whose address is in blocked_emails registers successfully as 'BLOCK@SpamFromHome.org' or 'Block@Spamfromhome.org'; should_block? returns false, no block error, and the entire feature is defeated by capitalizing one letter.

adjudication.rationale: `BlockedEmail.should_block?(email)` queries `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` (app/models/blocked_email.rb) with no normalization (e.g., downcasing) and no case-insensitive lookup. The new `EmailValidator` passes the raw user-provided email value into `should_block?` (lib/validators/email_validator.rb). From the diff alone, a blocked email stored as one case would not match a differently-cased registration input, allowing bypass on systems with case-sensitive string equality.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The validation path mutates and saves a different model (BlockedEmail#save inside should_block?) from within validate_each, so a failure of that write raises an unhandled ActiveRecord error during validation. If the BlockedEmail save fails (unique-index race on concurrent registration attempts, stale read-modify-write on match_count, or a validation failure on that row), the exception propagates out of user.save and the users#create rescue only catches StatementInvalid, turning a routine duplicate-signup into a 500 instead of the 4xx JSON error the endpoint returns elsewhere.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does introduce a side-effecting DB write during validation (`EmailValidator#validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, which does `record.save` after incrementing counters). However, the finding’s core claim—that a routine `save` failure will raise and propagate as an unhandled ActiveRecord exception turning common cases into 500s—is not supported by the shown code: `record.save` (not `save!`) normally returns false on validation failure rather than raising, and the cited “unique-index race on concurrent registration attempts” doesn’t apply because `should_block?` updates an existing `blocked_emails` row (it doesn’t insert one). The other cited failure modes (stale read-modify-write) also wouldn’t inherently raise. While DB errors could still raise in theory, that’s not verifiable from this diff and the specific scenarios described are misread.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] should_block? uses read-then-write (fetch, match_count += 1, save) with no lock, so concurrent signups for the same blocked email lose counter increments. match_count and last_match_at under-report actual block hits for the admin who loaded the table to observe blocking frequency; under concurrent spam bursts the statistics this feature exists to produce are silently wrong.

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, the code does a non-atomic read/modify/write (`where(...).first`, then `record.match_count += 1`, `record.last_match_at = ...`, `record.save`). Under concurrent signups hitting the same `blocked_emails.email`, updates can race and overwrite each other, losing increments and potentially last_match_at updates. This directly makes the new statistics (`match_count`, `last_match_at`) inaccurate under concurrency, which is a correctness defect in the added feature.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The client-side rejectedEmails check reports the failure with I18n.t('user.email.invalid') instead of the blocked-email message, while the server reports 'is not allowed.' A user whose email was blocked sees 'invalid' on subsequent keystrokes but a different message on submit — the inline hint misdirects them toward fixing a malformed address rather than using another one; misleading-error-content on the primary user-facing path of this feature.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a client-side cache `rejectedEmails` and, when an email is in that list, `emailValidation` returns a failed validation with `reason: I18n.t('user.email.invalid')` (create_account_controller.js). On submit failure, the controller pushes `result.values.email` into `rejectedEmails` whenever `result.errors.email` exists, regardless of the specific server-side error (also create_account_controller.js). Meanwhile the server introduces a distinct blocked-email validation message `user.email.blocked: "is not allowed."` via the new `EmailValidator` and locale entry (email_validator.rb, server.en.yml). This makes the inline validation message after a blocked-email failure incorrectly say “invalid” rather than “blocked/not allowed”, which is inconsistent and misleading behavior introduced by the new rejectedEmails path.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] rejectedEmails matching is an exact string comparison against result.values.email, so any retyped case variant or whitespace difference never matches the stored rejection and the client-side block never fires. A user blocked on 'bad@x.com' who edits the field to 'Bad@x.com' bypasses the inline validation, submits again, and burns a full server round-trip that re-rejects and pushes the new variant — a silent client/server desync where the added client validation is ineffective for exactly the input variations users produce.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a client-side cache of rejected emails: `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` in `emailMatch` (create_account_controller.js) and pushes `result.values.email` on failure. There is no normalization (trim/lowercase) on either the stored value or the current `accountEmail`, so case or whitespace variants won’t match and will still submit, relying on server-side validation. That’s a real, diff-grounded UX/perf gap in the new client-side optimization, but not a correctness/security defect because the server still rejects blocked/invalid emails.
